title: The Train Track That Bent in the Sun #shorts
sources: FRA / Railway Track & Structures (May 2023), 'Advanced Tools for Managing Continuous Welded Rail': welded rail is restrained from expanding and contracting; compressive forces in summer can cause track buckles, also called sun kinks; tensile forces in winter lead to pull-aparts; railroads want a high rail neutral temperature, so the rail is artificially lengthened by mechanical stretching or heating

FRA Safety Advisory 2012-03 (Federal Register, July 16, 2012): on July 4, 2012 a BNSF train crew noticed a sun kink ahead near Pendleton, Texas, tried to stop but could not, and 43 loaded coal cars derailed
Wikipedia, 'Rail stressing': before it is fixed, continuous welded rail is stretched with hydraulic tensors or heated to its stress-free temperature so it doesn't buckle in heat
WBTV (2010): before about 1950 rail came in 39-foot sections with room left at the joints for the steel to expand; heat 'slow orders' tell crews to go slowly over suspect track
